# Akamai Cloud Is Scaling for What Comes Next (Updated October 2026) 

 October 29, 2026 by Shawn Michels 

## Key takeaways 

We expanded NVIDIA RTX PRO™ 6000 Blackwell GPU capacity across our global cloud infrastructure and introduced 8-GPU configurations for larger AI inference, accelerated graphics, and simulation workloads.
Valkey Managed Database adds a high-performance, in-memory option for applications that depend on fast access to data, including AI applications that need caching, retrieval, and operational memory.
Updates to LKE Enterprise, LKE, and App Platform strengthen the foundation for running AI workloads at scale, with improvements to networking, application management, and day-to-day operations.
Reserved public IP addresses, placement group aware maintenance, private image sharing, single sign-on (SSO), and monitoring improvements give teams more control over how infrastructure is deployed and managed.

...

In Q1, we expanded our AI infrastructure with NVIDIA RTX PRO™ 6000 Blackwell GPUs and introduced Akamai Functions.

...

This quarter, we expanded our NVIDIA RTX PRO™ 6000 Blackwell GPU infrastructure with new 8-GPU configurations. The additional GPU and VRAM capacity gives you more room to run larger models; supports longer context windows; and handles demanding language, multimodal, graphics, and simulation workloads. We’ve also recently made available Akamai B300 GPU, powered by NVIDIA HGX B300 with Blackwell Ultra GPUs.

At the same time, we continued expanding GPU capacity across our global cloud infrastructure. As more organizations move AI into production, they need access to accelerated compute in the markets where they operate. Our global footprint puts us in a unique position to support that expansion, giving you greater flexibility in where and how you deploy AI workloads.

The direction is straightforward: Give customers more choices for how much accelerated compute they need and give them more places to run it.

results.title: What Is a Cloud GPU? | Akamai
highlights:
## Cloud GPU pricing and options 

When it comes to cloud GPU pricing, it’s important to understand the different models available. The cost of renting a (lower-cost) NVIDIA RTX™ 6000, for example, can vary depending on the provider and the specific configuration. On-demand pricing is a popular model that allows users to pay only for the resources they use, making it a cost-effective solution for start-ups and small businesses. This model is particularly useful for projects with variable workloads, as it enables users to scale resources up or down as needed.

For larger enterprises, subscription-based pricing models may be more suitable. These models often offer discounted rates for long-term commitments, making them a cost-effective solution for organizations with consistent and predictable workloads. Providers such as Akamai Cloud, Google Cloud, AWS, and Oracle Cloud offer a range of pricing options, including on-demand, reserved, and spot instances, to cater to different budget and performance requirements.

## Cost analysis 

When comparing the costs of different cloud GPU instances, it’s essential to consider factors such as the type of GPU, the amount of memory, and the bandwidth. For example, the NVIDIA RTX 4000 GPU is a high-performance option that is well suited for deep learning and HPC workloads. The cost of renting high-performance GPU per hour can vary, but it is generally more expensive than lower-end GPUs. However, the performance benefits often justify the higher cost, especially for large-scale simulations and complex AI models.

The B200 (Blackwell) is another advanced GPU that offers even greater computational power and efficiency. While the B200 is more expensive, it can provide significant performance improvements, making it a cost-effective choice for organizations with demanding workloads. When evaluating the cost of cloud GPU instances, it’s important to consider the total cost of ownership, including factors such as power consumption, cooling, and maintenance, which can add to the overall cost of on-premises solutions.

...

## Pricing models 

Cloud providers offer a variety of pricing models to cater to different needs and budgets. On-demand pricing is a flexible model that allows users to pay for GPU resources as they use them. This model is ideal for projects with unpredictable workloads or for organizations that want to avoid long-term commitments. On-demand pricing ensures that users only pay for the resources they consume, making it a cost-effective solution for start-ups and small businesses.

Subscription-based pricing models, on the other hand, offer discounted rates for long-term commitments. These models are suitable for enterprises with consistent and predictable workloads, as they can provide more stable and predictable costs. Providers such as Akamai, AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure offer various subscription options, including reserved instances and savings plans, which can help organizations optimize their cloud spending.

...

## What are the different pricing models for cloud GPUs?

Cloud providers offer various pricing models for cloud GPUs, including on-demand pricing, subscription-based pricing, reserved instances, and spot instances. On-demand pricing allows users to pay for GPU resources as they use them, while subscription-based models offer discounted rates for long-term commitments.

results.title: Oct 28, 2026 — IPv4 limits
highlights:
Oct 28, 2026 — IPv4 limits

# Oct 28, 2026 — IPv4 limits

 17 days ago 

Akamai Cloud now applies account-level IPv4 allocation limits in each data center. These limits help protect IPv4 address availability by preventing a single account from using up a data center's IPv4 inventory, ensuring reliable and predictable provisioning for all customer accounts.

Affected resources

IPv4 limits apply to new public and private IPv4 allocations, including allocations for:

- Linode instances
- NodeBalancers
- Linode Kubernetes Engine (LKE / LKE-E) nodes
- Managed Databases
- Reserved IPs
- Additional IP addresses

Existing resources and existing IPv4 assignments are not affected.

...

Exceeding IPv4 limits

If a new allocation request causes your account to exceed its IPv4 quota in a given data center, the provisioning request will be denied and details such as the reason for the denial, current usage, the applicable limit, and the data center's region (for example, us-east) are provided.

If your application requires additional IPv4 capacity in a specific data center, you can request an account limit increase by opening a ticket with Customer Support and include the following details:

- The data center where you need the increase.
- The requested limit.
- A brief business justification.
- Expected growth over the next 6–12 months, if available.

Limit increase requests are reviewed based on your use case and available capacity in the requested data center.

# Dreadfully slow upload?
stolk 5 years, 4 months ago
I am uploading a file to my nano node, and I am seeing dreadful bandwidth.
It uploads with 140KB/sec.
My Internet speed is a lot more than that.
I tested my upload speed which came back as 6.4Mbps, so 700KB/sec should easily be doable?
What is going on?
What BW should I expect for a nano node?
The CPU is idle, btw.
It is running in Fremont, CA. I am in Vancouver, BC.
### 2 Replies
jdutton 5 years, 4 months ago Linode Staff
Network throughput speeds can be affected by a ton of factors, including network conditions at the time of the upload. Your best bet will be to compare your actual upload/download speeds with a speed test here and run some MTR reports to and from the source you're connecting to.
If you're not familiar, MTR reports will show you the network route being taken between two points, as well as any network issues along the way (i.e. packet loss, latency). For reference, the below links have tips on installing, using, and deciphering MTR reports:
In terms of what to expect, the maximum throughput for a Nanode is listed on our pricing page: 40 Gbps in, 1000 Mbps out. However, this is entirely dependent on network conditions, ISP reliability/outages, number of shared connections, connection type, processes running on your local machine + the remote machine, RAM allocation, etc.
